goal_text: How to choose between RAG and fine-tuning

nodes.title: What is RAG, in plain terms?
nodes.one_liner: Retrieval + generation: giving a model external facts to answer from.

nodes.title: What is fine-tuning, in plain terms?
nodes.one_liner: Retraining a model to change how it behaves or responds.

nodes.title: The core difference: knowledge vs. behavior
nodes.one_liner: RAG adds facts; fine-tuning shapes style and skills.

nodes.title: What kind of problem are you solving?
nodes.one_liner: Which use cases naturally favor RAG vs. fine-tuning.

nodes.title: What does your data look like?
nodes.one_liner: Volume, freshness, and format that push each way.

nodes.title: Cost, effort, and maintenance compared
nodes.one_liner: Upfront work vs. ongoing upkeep for each approach.

nodes.title: A decision checklist for your project
nodes.one_liner: Concrete questions that point you to a choice.

nodes.title: When to combine both
nodes.one_liner: Why hybrid setups are common and when they help.

outline.rationale: The user is new to both concepts and needs to make a practical decision for a real project. I lead with two brief definition nodes (RAG, fine-tuning) since no prior background is assumed, then a single node crystallizing the core conceptual distinction (knowledge vs. behavior) — this is the minimal mechanics needed to understand tradeoffs, matching the request to deprioritize deep internals. The middle nodes are the practical decision factors explicitly promised: use-case type, data characteristics, and cost/maintenance — kept MECE (data vs. cost vs. use case don't overlap). The checklist node makes the decision actionable for their actual project, and the hybrid node prevents the false-dichotomy trap since combining both is common in practice. I excluded history, embedding math, training internals, and implementation tutorials as beyond decision-making needs.
